docker.title: Postgres superuser password has a weak dev default that is not generated by op-init on first run
docker.description: The PostgreSQL container has POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-dev_postgres_superuser}. While op-init generates a strong password file (db_password_postgres_superuser.txt), this is only used by set-passwords.sh to ALTER ROLE. The initial POSTGRES_PASSWORD env var used during postgres container initialization still defaults to the weak 'dev_postgres_superuser' string unless the operator manually sets POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env. The prod compose file does enforce this, but the base compose with the weak default could be mistakenly used in production.

docker.title: Docker socket proxy enables POST and DELETE capabilities for container management
docker.description: The docker-socket-proxy has CONTAINERS=1, IMAGES=1, POST=1, DELETE=1, and LOG=1 enabled. While this is necessary for the execution service to manage sandbox containers, the POST and DELETE permissions combined with CONTAINERS access allow creating and deleting arbitrary containers. If the execution service or sandbox network is compromised, an attacker could create privileged containers or delete other services' containers. The proxy lacks fine-grained path filtering to restrict operations to sandbox containers only.

docker.title: Init script writes secret files with world-readable permissions (0444)
docker.description: All secret files (master key, JWT secret, database passwords, Ed25519 private keys) are written with chmod 0444 (world-readable). The comment explains this is necessary because service containers run as UID 1001 and postgres as UID 70, and the volume is mounted :ro. However, 0444 means any process in any container that mounts init-data can read every secret file, not just its own. A compromised app-service container could read the auth-service's database password, the master encryption key, and all Ed25519 private keys.

packages/app-sdk.title: QueryCache.invalidate() deletes entries while iterating over entries.keys()
packages/app-sdk.description: The invalidate() method iterates over this.entries.keys() and calls this.entries.delete(key) inside the loop. While the ES2015 Map spec guarantees that deleting the current key during iteration is safe and the iterator will not revisit deleted keys, this pattern depends on a subtle spec guarantee that is easy to break during refactoring. If someone were to change the iteration to use a cached array or different collection type, it could silently skip entries or throw.

packages/app-sdk.title: withRetry performs 4 total attempts but BFF_MAX_RETRIES=3 implies 3 total
packages/app-sdk.description: The retry loop condition is 'attempt <= BFF_MAX_RETRIES' with attempt starting at 0 and BFF_MAX_RETRIES=3, resulting in 4 total attempts (indices 0, 1, 2, 3). The constant name 'BFF_MAX_RETRIES' and the JSDoc 'up to BFF_MAX_RETRIES times' suggest the intent is 3 total attempts (1 initial + 2 retries), not 4 (1 initial + 3 retries). The exponential backoff delays are computed as 500ms, 1000ms, 2000ms which match 3 retries, but the loop actually allows a fourth attempt at 4000ms delay.

packages/cli.title: Silent fallback to machine-id decryption when keychain entry is missing -- masks credential theft
packages/cli.description: In decryptEntry(), when a credential was stored with keyDerivation='keychain' but the keychain entry is missing (e.g., deleted or on a different machine), the code silently falls through to machine-id derivation (line 240-241). Since the credential was encrypted with a random 32-byte key stored in the keychain, decrypting with the machine-id derived key will always fail with a crypto error. However, the intent to silently fall through means no warning is issued about the missing keychain entry. Worse, if an attacker replaces the credentials.json and changes keyDerivation to 'machine-id' while copying the file to a machine where they control machine-id, the fallback would successfully decrypt without any warning. The fallback should either not exist for keychain-encrypted credentials, or should at minimum issue a clear warning.

packages/cli.title: parseConfigDocuments accepts any string as ResourceKind without validation
packages/cli.description: The YAML parser casts d['kind'] directly to ResourceKind without validating it is one of the six known kinds (Role, Ontology, Connector, Pipeline, App, Webhook). If a user provides a YAML document with kind: 'Unknown', it will be accepted as a ConfigDocument but will have no dependency edges in DEPS and no priority in KIND_PRIORITY (defaulting to 99). This means invalid kinds silently pass through parsing and topological sort, only failing later at import time with a confusing server error.

packages/cli.title: Interactive login sends credentials using the old profile's HTTP client (without auth or with wrong platform URL)
packages/cli.description: In loginAction's interactive mode (no --key), the email/password POST is made via ctx.http which was constructed by the preAction hook using the current profile's credentials and platform URL. If the user has not yet logged in (credentials are null), the HTTP client has no auth header -- which is correct for a login endpoint. However, if the user provides --platform to override the URL, ctx.http still points at the OLD platformUrl (from the pre-action hook's resolution), not the overridden URL. The --platform override is applied to opts.platform (line 31) but only used for key-based login (line 41-51); the interactive path at line 59 uses ctx.http which was constructed before the override.

packages/cli.title: user get renders a single object through render() with columns, which expects an array
packages/cli.description: In getAction, ctx.renderer.render(user, USER_COLUMNS) is called with a single user object (not wrapped in an array). The render() method checks Array.isArray(data) to decide on table/tsv rendering (output.ts lines 161-174). Since a single object is not an array, it will always fall through to renderJson() regardless of the output format. Meanwhile, the connectors and pipelines get commands correctly wrap in an array: `ctx.renderer.render([connector], CONNECTOR_COLUMNS)`. This inconsistency means `op user get <id> -o table` always outputs JSON.

packages/cli.title: Plugin rollback ignores --yes flag, always prompts for confirmation
packages/cli.description: rollbackAction checks `if (!ctx.yes)` and then calls confirmDestructive with `false` as the yes parameter (line 194). This means even when `--yes` is passed globally, the confirmation prompt still appears because the hardcoded `false` overrides ctx.yes. The correct pattern (used elsewhere, e.g., dlq discard) is to pass ctx.yes to confirmDestructive.

packages/cli.title: Plugin install ignores --yes flag, always prompts non-dev installations
packages/cli.description: installAction checks `ctx.yes` on line 126 and prints a warning, but the else branch on line 129 calls `confirmDestructive('Install plugin ...?', false)` with a hardcoded `false`, ignoring ctx.yes. This means --yes does produce a warning but the prompt still appears because confirmDestructive receives false. The auto-approve message on line 127 is misleading since confirmation is not actually bypassed.

packages/cli.title: Plugin upgrade ignores --yes flag, always prompts for confirmation
packages/cli.description: upgradeAction checks `if (!ctx.yes)` and then calls confirmDestructive with `false` as the yes parameter. Same issue as the rollback command -- even with --yes, the prompt still appears because confirmDestructive receives false.

packages/core.title: Core health.ts readyz returns "not-ready" (hyphen) while all custom health routes return "not_ready" (underscore)
packages/core.description: The core package's readyz() function returns status: "not-ready" (with a hyphen) while the custom health routes in app, execution, gateway, ingestion, pipeline, and plugin services all return status: "not_ready" (with an underscore). Auth, ontology, and logging use the core healthz/readyz directly, so they return "not-ready". Any monitoring tool or orchestrator parsing the readyz response to check service readiness will get inconsistent values depending on which service it queries.

packages/core.title: Response envelope middleware skips wrapping any response containing a 'data' key, preventing routes from returning objects with 'data' as a domain field
packages/core.description: The middleware checks `"data" in (body as object)` to detect already-enveloped responses and skip double-wrapping. However, this means if a route handler returns a domain object that naturally has a 'data' field (e.g. { data: [...], metadata: {...} } or { data: 'raw content', format: 'csv' }), the middleware assumes it is already enveloped and does not wrap it. The consumer would receive { data: [...], metadata: {...} } instead of the expected { data: { data: [...], metadata: {...} } }. This is a semantic ambiguity that can cause subtle frontend breakage when domain models use 'data' as a field name.

packages/frontend.title: Webhook URL validation rejects valid HTTPS URLs that contain 'http://' as a substring
packages/frontend.description: The webhook URL validation uses z.string().url() followed by .refine(val => !val.startsWith('http://'), ...). The .url() validator accepts any valid URL including http:// URLs. The refine then rejects URLs starting with 'http://'. However, the error message says 'Webhook URLs must use HTTPS' but the validation does not positively check for https:// -- it only rejects http://. This means non-http, non-https schemes like ftp://, file://, or custom schemes would pass validation but likely fail at delivery time.

packages/frontend.title: describeCron produces incorrect ordinal suffixes for days 11-13 and 21-23
packages/frontend.description: The describeCron function generates ordinal suffixes for day-of-month values but only handles '1st', '2nd', '3rd' explicitly and uses 'th' for everything else. This works for most numbers but produces wrong output for '21st' (shows '21th'), '22nd' (shows '22th'), '23rd' (shows '23th'), and correctly handles 11th/12th/13th by accident (since they are not 1/2/3). For days 21, 22, 23, 31 the output is grammatically incorrect.

packages/plugin-sdk.title: HookPayloadDataMap maps before:pipeline.complete to PipelineCompleteData which documents itself as after-only
packages/plugin-sdk.description: PipelineCompleteData (line 224) has a JSDoc comment stating it is 'Available to `after:pipeline.complete` only -- at this point all steps have either succeeded or failed.' However, HookPayloadDataMap maps both `before:pipeline.complete` and `after:pipeline.complete` to PipelineCompleteData. The data shape includes `status`, `duration`, and `stepResults` which would not be available in the 'before' stage since the pipeline has not actually completed yet. This type mismatch could lead plugin authors to rely on fields like `status` in a before hook where they would not have meaningful values.

packages/plugin-sdk.title: Widget scaffold template inserts user-controlled values into HTML without escaping
packages/plugin-sdk.description: The scaffolded widget render() method interpolates `title` (from data.config) and `data.user.id` directly into an HTML template string without HTML entity escaping. While the SDK docs mention DOMPurify is applied server-side, the scaffold teaches an unsafe pattern that developers may replicate when building real widgets. A malicious config title containing '<script>' or HTML entities could inject content if the server-side sanitization is ever bypassed or misconfigured.

packages/plugin-sdk.title: Timeout timer in timedCall is never cleared when the actual call resolves first
packages/plugin-sdk.description: In the timedCall function, Promise.race is used between fn() and timeoutPromise(). When fn() resolves/rejects before the timeout, the setTimeout in timeoutPromise is never cleared. While unref() prevents it from keeping the process alive, the timer callback still fires after the timeout period, calling reject() on an already-settled promise. Over many fetchBatch iterations (up to maxBatches=100), this accumulates dangling timers.

packages/sdk.title: Transport unwraps {data: T} envelope incorrectly - falsy data values silently dropped
packages/sdk.description: The envelope unwrapping logic at lines 470-476 checks `if (envelope.data !== undefined && envelope.data !== null)` and returns envelope.data when truthy. But when the server returns `{data: 0}`, `{data: false}`, or `{data: ""}` (legitimate responses for count endpoints, boolean toggles, etc.), the check passes for 0 and false and empty-string since they are not undefined/null, so those are returned correctly. However, the same logic exists in `executeMultipartRequest` (line 347) and the two copies could diverge. More importantly, if the server response has no `data` key at all (e.g. `{items: [...], nextCursor: null}`) the code falls through to `return parsed as T`, which works. But if the server returns `{data: null}` to explicitly mean 'no result', the code falls through and returns the entire envelope `{data: null}` as type T instead of returning null. Callers expecting `T | null` get an object with a data property instead.

packages/sdk.title: PKCE callback code/state extracted at module scope but never auto-processed
packages/sdk.description: At PKCE handler construction time (lines 243-252), the code extracts `code` and `state` from the current URL query params and strips them via `history.replaceState`. However, the extracted `callbackCode` and `callbackState` variables are never used -- they are local variables that are discarded. The caller must separately call `handleCallback(window.location.href)` to actually exchange the code. But by the time they call it, the code/state have already been stripped from the URL (line 250), so `handleCallback` will fail because the URL no longer contains the params. The caller would need to save the original URL before creating the client.

packages/sdk.title: Default retry policy retries on NetworkError status codes but NetworkError has no statusCode
packages/sdk.description: In the transport's `request()` method (line 239), the retry logic uses `getStatusCode` which extracts `err.statusCode` from OnePlatformError instances. However, NetworkError sets statusCode to undefined (since the request never reached the server). The retry handler's `withRetry` at retry-handler.ts line 111 checks `if (status === undefined || !policy.retryableStatusCodes.includes(status))` -- when status is undefined, it throws immediately without retrying. This means timeout errors and connection failures (NetworkError with reason 'timeout' or 'fetch-failed') are NEVER retried, despite NetworkError having `retryable = true`. The retry mechanism only retries on HTTP status codes, not on network-level failures.

packages/sdk.title: PKCE URL stripping drops query parameters unrelated to auth callback
packages/sdk.description: When stripping the OAuth callback params from the URL, the code replaces the entire URL with just `pathname + hash`, discarding ALL query parameters -- not just `code` and `state`. If the application URL contained other query parameters (e.g., `?code=abc&state=xyz&tab=settings&view=dashboard`), the `tab` and `view` params are also lost. This can break application routing or state management that relies on query parameters.

packages/sdk.title: DataNamespace Proxy intercepts built-in property accesses, may break debugging tools
packages/sdk.description: The Proxy handler for `client.data` intercepts ALL string property accesses (line 235) and returns an EntityResource for any string property that is not 'entity'. This means accessing `client.data.then`, `client.data.toJSON`, `client.data.constructor`, or `client.data[Symbol.toStringTag]` all return EntityResource instances for entity types named 'then', 'toJSON', etc. This is particularly problematic for `.then` because it makes `client.data` look like a thenable to Promise.resolve() and await, causing unexpected behavior: `await client.data` would attempt to call `client.data.then()` which is an EntityResource object (not a function), causing a confusing error.

plugins/auth-provider-ldap.title: Whitespace-only password bypasses empty-password check, enabling anonymous LDAP bind
plugins/auth-provider-ldap.description: The password validation checks `password === ""` (exact empty string) but the username validation uses `username.trim() === ""`. A password consisting entirely of whitespace (e.g., " " or "\t") passes this check and is sent to the LDAP proxy as the bind password. Many LDAP servers treat whitespace-only passwords the same as empty passwords, performing an anonymous bind that succeeds without credential verification. This is a credential bypass vulnerability: an attacker who knows a valid username can authenticate by supplying a whitespace-only password.

plugins/auth-provider-ldap.title: configSchema in metadata() marks bindCredentialKey as required but parseConfig provides a default
plugins/auth-provider-ldap.description: The configSchema in metadata() lists 'bindCredentialKey' in the 'required' array (line 528), which means the platform's JSON Schema validation will reject any configuration that omits this field. However, parseConfig (line 135) provides a default value of 'ldap_bind_password' when bindCredentialKey is missing or empty. This creates an inconsistency: the schema validation will reject configs before parseConfig ever gets a chance to apply its default. The manifest (plugin.manifest.json line 15) also lists it as required. Either the default in parseConfig is dead code, or the schema should not mark it as required.

plugins/auth-provider-oidc.title: additionalParams can override security-critical OAuth parameters
plugins/auth-provider-oidc.description: The additionalParams from AuthOptions are applied via params.set() after all security-critical parameters (response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state) are set. Since URLSearchParams.set() replaces existing keys, a caller passing additionalParams with keys like 'response_type', 'client_id', 'redirect_uri', or 'state' can override the secure defaults. For example, setting response_type to 'token' would switch to the implicit flow, bypassing PKCE/code-exchange security.

plugins/auth-provider-oidc.title: djb2 hash function uses signed 32-bit arithmetic, producing negative intermediate values
plugins/auth-provider-oidc.description: The hashString function uses the djb2 algorithm with bitwise operators. In JavaScript, `hash << 5` operates on signed 32-bit integers, and the XOR with charCodeAt can produce negative values. While `hash >>> 0` at the end converts to unsigned, the intermediate signed overflow behavior means that hash values wrap around at 2^31 rather than 2^32 during computation. This does not cause a crash but means the hash distribution is slightly different from the canonical unsigned djb2, and for very long strings the intermediate values could produce collisions that the unsigned variant would not.

plugins/connector-csv.title: Multi-character delimiters silently accepted but cause incorrect parsing
plugins/connector-csv.description: The delimiter config is validated only as a non-empty string (line 240). The parser compares single characters against the delimiter via text[pos] === delimiter (lines 149, 164, 171). In JavaScript, text[pos] returns a single character; comparing it to a multi-character string with === always returns false. A multi-character delimiter like '||' or '::' will never be detected: all fields merge into one giant field per row. The data is silently corrupted with no error reported.

plugins/connector-csv.title: All fetch exceptions misclassified as PluginTimeoutError, including permanent failures
plugins/connector-csv.description: When context.fetch.fetch() throws during the GET request in fetchBatch (line 401-403), every exception is wrapped as PluginTimeoutError. PluginTimeoutError has isRetryable=true, meaning the platform will retry these failures with backoff. However, many fetch exceptions are permanent (e.g., PluginAuthError from FetchProxy for disallowed URLs, DNS resolution failures for misspelled domains, SSL certificate errors). Wrapping them all as retryable timeout errors causes the platform to pointlessly retry failures that will never succeed, wasting ingestion worker time and delaying error surfacing.

plugins/connector-mysql.title: IPv4 regex capture groups mapped via .map(Number) includes the full match, producing NaN comparison
plugins/connector-mysql.description: The destructuring 'const [, a, b] = ipv4Match.map(Number)' maps the entire match array through Number(), including ipv4Match[0] which is the full match string (e.g., '192.168.1.1'). Number('192.168.1.1') returns NaN. This is harmless because the destructuring skips index 0 via the leading comma, but it is misleading code. More importantly, for the check 'b !== undefined' on line 166, b can never be undefined because the regex has 4 capture groups and will always produce indices 0-4. The check is dead code that obscures a potential issue: b could theoretically be NaN if the regex matched a non-numeric octet, though the \d+ pattern prevents that.

plugins/connector-postgres.title: handleToConfig nullish coalescing allows batchSize=0 to pass through unchecked
plugins/connector-postgres.description: The batchSize rehydration uses nullish coalescing: '(m["batchSize"] as number) ?? DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE'. The ?? operator only catches null/undefined, not 0. If handle.metadata contains batchSize=0 (due to corruption or manual manipulation), it passes through as 0. This results in 'limit=0' being sent to the proxy, which could return all rows (unbounded query) or zero rows depending on proxy implementation, creating either a performance bomb or silent data loss.

plugins/connector-rest-api.title: Invalid cursor logged in error message may leak sensitive pagination state
plugins/connector-rest-api.description: When decodeCursor fails, the error message includes the raw cursor string value. In some API integrations, cursor tokens may contain sensitive information (session tokens, internal IDs, or encoded query parameters). Including the raw cursor in the error message means it will be logged by the platform's error handling, potentially exposing sensitive data to anyone with log access.

plugins/connector-rest-api.title: POST requests never send a request body
plugins/connector-rest-api.description: The connector supports method: 'POST' but the fetch call at line 557 never includes a body in the request. Many REST APIs that use POST for querying expect a JSON body with filter/pagination parameters. The connector only passes parameters as URL query strings regardless of the HTTP method. For APIs that expect POST with a JSON body (e.g., Elasticsearch _search, GraphQL endpoints), the connector will send an empty-body POST which will likely return an error or default unfiltered results.

plugins/connector-webhook.title: hasMore=true with nextCursor=null when all page records are skipped
plugins/connector-webhook.description: When all payloads in a page are skipped (failed HMAC verification or TTL-expired), lastSuccessfulId remains null (initialized on line 547, only updated on line 548 for successfully mapped records). The nextCursor is computed as 'hasMore ? lastSuccessfulId : null' on line 617. If hasMore is true (there are more IDs beyond this page in the original index) but every record in this page was skipped, nextCursor becomes null despite hasMore being true. This violates the BatchResult contract (documented in connector.ts line 40: 'Set to true if there are more records after this batch (i.e., nextCursor is non-null)'). The ingestion service, seeing nextCursor=null, will either stop fetching (causing data loss of remaining valid payloads) or restart from the beginning (causing an infinite retry loop if the same payloads keep failing).

plugins/connector-webhook.title: estimatedTotal reports stale count that does not account for skipped/removed payloads
plugins/connector-webhook.description: The estimatedTotal field on line 635 is set to allIds.length, which is the count from the initial snapshot before any processing. After the batch completes, the actual remaining count is remainingIds.length (computed on line 605), which may be significantly smaller because processed IDs (including skipped ones) were removed. The estimatedTotal is documented as advisory (connector.ts line 50: 'The platform never makes correctness decisions based on this value'), but it would show misleading progress in the UI -- e.g., showing 100 total when only 3 remain after processing 97 in a previous batch.

services/app.title: validateFilePath rejects files without extensions despite .env.example being in allowed list
services/app.description: The validateFilePath function extracts the extension using path.slice(path.lastIndexOf('.')). For the allowed extension '.env.example', a file at '/config/.env.example' would have lastIndexOf('.') point at '.example', yielding ext='.example' which is NOT in the allowed set. The intended extension '.env.example' can never be matched by this logic because lastIndexOf('.') only captures the last dot-delimited segment. Any file intended to use the '.env.example' extension would be rejected with an invalid path error.

services/auth.title: API key service getBcryptRounds lacks NaN guard, could produce invalid hashes
services/auth.description: getBcryptRounds() (line 79-82) parses OP_BCRYPT_ROUNDS with parseInt but has no NaN check. If the env var is set to a non-numeric value, parseInt returns NaN, which is then passed to bcrypt.hash(fullKey, NaN). Depending on the bcrypt library version, this could throw an unhandled error during key creation or produce a hash with unpredictable cost factor. The password-service.ts version (lines 15-32) properly validates and rejects values below the minimum threshold, but this copy does not.

services/auth.title: OAuth callback schema requires code even when error is present
services/auth.description: The oauthCallbackQuery schema (line 283) defines `code: z.string()` as required and `error: z.string().optional()`. When an OAuth provider denies consent, it redirects back with `?error=access_denied` but without a `code` parameter. The schema validation will fail because code is required, preventing the route from reaching the error-handling logic (lines 60-64 of oauth.ts) that converts provider-side denials into a proper error response. The user would see a generic 'Invalid OAuth callback query' validation error instead of the meaningful 'OAuth provider returned an error' message.

services/execution.title: recordRun adds execution to inflightIds even when sandbox is DRAINING_OLD
services/execution.description: recordRun() unconditionally adds the executionId to primary.inflightIds and increments runCount without checking the sandbox state. If recordRun is called after getPrimary() returned successfully but triggerRecycle() ran in between (e.g., the recycle timer fired), the new execution is added to inflightIds while the drain is already in progress. The drain's waitForInflightDrain will then wait for or force-kill this execution that was just dispatched, causing unexpected execution failures.

services/execution.title: Connector run uses empty string as code when plugin bundle fetch returns null
services/execution.description: In runConnectorExecution, if the plugin bundle cache returns null (bundle not found or fetch failed), the code falls through to execute with `bundle?.bundleBase64 ?? ''` (empty string). This sends an empty code payload to the sandbox which will either crash or produce a cryptic error, rather than failing fast with a clear 'plugin bundle not found' error.

services/gateway.title: Billing webhook config lacks authorization scope check
services/gateway.description: The POST, GET, and DELETE endpoints for /api/v1/billing/webhook-config only check that the user is authenticated (has a tenantId) but do not verify any specific scope or role. Any authenticated user within a tenant can create, view, or delete the billing webhook configuration, including setting arbitrary webhook URLs and thresholds. In contrast, other sensitive admin operations (rate limits, data residency, transfer rules) require the 'admin' scope. This allows a low-privilege user to configure billing webhooks that fire to an attacker-controlled endpoint and receive internal usage data.

services/gateway.title: In-memory rate-limit and SSE maps are module-level singletons that leak across tests and hot reloads
services/gateway.description: The inMemoryWindows map in sliding-window-rate-limiter.ts (line 102) is a module-level global. While the SSE service creates its buffers map inside the factory function (correctly scoped), the rate limiter's fallback map persists across all createSlidingWindowLimiter calls. In test environments or hot-reload scenarios, stale entries accumulate across test runs. In production with a single process this is benign, but it violates the factory pattern used elsewhere and could cause test flakiness.

services/gateway.title: Introspection query detector returns true for mixed queries containing both __schema and data fields
services/gateway.description: The isIntrospectionQuery function returns true if ANY selection in any query operation is __schema or __type. This means a query like '{ __schema { types { name } } users { id } }' would be identified as an introspection query, causing the entire query to be handled by the introspection handler instead of executing the 'users' resolver. The user would receive only introspection data and silently lose the 'users' result.

services/gateway.title: GraphQL write scope check uses 'write' but the platform uses 'data:write' scopes
services/gateway.description: The assertWritePermission function checks for scopes 'write' or 'admin' in the WRITE_SCOPES set. However, the data route handler (routes/data.ts line 43) checks for 'data:write' scope for mutating operations. This inconsistency means the GraphQL endpoint may grant write access to users with a bare 'write' scope while denying it to users with 'data:write', or vice versa. The webhook routes use 'webhooks:manage', lineage uses 'lineage:read' - the scoping pattern across the gateway is 'domain:action', not bare 'write'.

services/ingestion.title: HMAC verification bypass via truncated signature
services/ingestion.description: The HMAC verification copies the incoming hex-decoded signature into a fixed-size buffer via Buffer.copy, which silently truncates to the expected length. The subsequent timingSafeEqual compares only the first N bytes. The length check `incomingHex.length === expectedHmac.length` is performed AFTER timingSafeEqual, but the order of the `&&` operator means timingSafeEqual must pass first. However, the real issue is that `Buffer.from(incomingHex, 'hex')` on a string shorter than expectedHmac produces a shorter buffer that is zero-padded by Buffer.alloc. If the attacker sends a signature that happens to match the first few bytes of the expected HMAC when zero-padded, timingSafeEqual would pass. While the subsequent length check would catch this, the comparison `incomingHex.length === expectedHmac.length` compares the *hex string* lengths, not the raw buffer lengths. An attacker sending the correct hex characters plus extra non-hex characters (which Buffer.from('hex') silently ignores) could potentially make incomingHex.length match expectedHmac.length while the actual decoded bytes are different. For example, 'abcdzz' has length 6 but Buffer.from('abcdzz','hex') produces only 2 bytes (0xab, 0xcd). This could allow forgery if an attacker crafts a hex string with the right length but invalid hex characters after the valid prefix.

services/ingestion.title: Schema inference off-by-one: schema only inferred when exactly SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS records parsed
services/ingestion.description: The schema inference check on line 305 triggers only when `rowsParsed === SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS` (i.e., exactly 200). If the file has fewer than 200 records, inferredSchema is never set and no schema is written to the upload job. For files with fewer than 200 records, users see a null inferredSchema even though there are records available for inference. The check should be `rowsParsed >= SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS` or should trigger at end-of-file when rowsParsed < SCHEMA_INFERENCE_ROWS.

services/ingestion.title: ForbiddenError leaks connector existence to cross-tenant users
services/ingestion.description: In requireConnectorForTenant, when a connector exists but belongs to a different tenant, the code throws ForbiddenError('You do not have access to connector X'). This is an information leak: a user in tenant A can probe connector IDs and distinguish between 'connector does not exist' (ConnectorNotFoundError) and 'connector exists but belongs to another tenant' (ForbiddenError) by observing the HTTP status code difference (404 vs 403). This violates the principle of not revealing resource existence to unauthorized users.

services/ingestion.title: Connector ID path parameter not validated as UUID before database lookup
services/ingestion.description: The `:id` path parameter in GET/PATCH/DELETE /:id routes is passed directly to connectorService.getConnector without any UUID format validation. While the pg driver will reject non-UUID strings with a database error, the error message will be a raw PostgreSQL error (e.g., 'invalid input syntax for type uuid') rather than a clean validation error. This affects all connector routes using c.req.param('id'), as well as webhook and upload routes.

services/pipeline.title: Timer leak in evaluateWithTimeout — setTimeout never cleared on success
services/pipeline.description: The evaluateWithTimeout function uses Promise.race between the jsonata evaluation and a setTimeout-based timeout. When the evaluation completes successfully (the normal path), the setTimeout timer is never cleared. This happens for every webhook body template evaluation and every responseMapping evaluation. Over many pipeline runs, this creates thousands of orphaned timers that each hold closures referencing the reject function and potentially large data.

services/pipeline.title: SSE log stream uses stale initial run status for terminal check — may close prematurely or miss final logs
services/pipeline.description: The SSE log stream handler fetches the run status once at line 54, then uses it to decide whether to close the stream at line 105. If the run transitions to terminal status between the initial fetch and the log retrieval, the stream may close before all final log entries are captured. Conversely, if the run is fetched as 'running' but becomes terminal between the status check and the follow-loop entry, the stream enters the poll loop and catches it on the next iteration — which is correct but shows the initial check is redundant in a racy way.

services/pipeline.title: buildAdjacencyMap does not recurse into parallel branch steps for cycle detection
services/pipeline.description: The buildAdjacencyMap function only processes top-level steps. When a parallel step contains branches with nested steps, only the entryStepId of each branch is added as a neighbor of the parallel step, but the steps inside the branches are not added to the adjacency map. This means cycles within parallel branches (e.g., a conditional step inside a branch that points back to the parallel step) would not be detected by hasCycle.

services/plugin.title: Cache DELETE endpoint missing key validation present in GET/PUT
services/plugin.description: The GET (line 178) and PUT (line 205) cache endpoints validate the key parameter with: key.length > 256 || !/^[\w\-.:]+$/.test(key). The DELETE endpoint at line 234 does not perform this validation, accepting any key value. While this is an internal endpoint protected by service token auth, the inconsistency means a malformed key could be injected into the Redis key string (plugin:cache:{tenantId}:{pluginId}:{key}). Although Redis key injection is limited in impact, it breaks the security-in-depth pattern the other endpoints follow.

services/plugin.title: In-memory rate limiter Map grows unboundedly
services/plugin.description: The token bucket rate limiter stores an entry in a Map for every unique userId that makes a publish or rate request. These entries are never evicted. Over the lifetime of the process, the Map will grow without bound. With many users, this will consume increasing memory. The buckets Map is module-scoped and shared across all requests.

services/plugin.title: Ratings cursor pagination uses id > cursor with DESC ordering, producing incorrect results
services/plugin.description: In findRatingsByPlugin, the cursor-based pagination uses 'AND id > $2' (line 295) as the cursor condition, but the ORDER BY is 'created_at DESC, id DESC' (line 296). For descending pagination, the cursor condition should use '<' (less than) to get the next page of results. Using '>' with DESC order will skip results or return results from the wrong direction, effectively showing unpredictable pages when the cursor is applied.

services/plugin.title: executeAtomicSwap does BEGIN/COMMIT without try/catch ROLLBACK
services/plugin.description: The executeAtomicSwap function calls client.query("BEGIN") and later client.query("COMMIT"), but if any query between BEGIN and COMMIT throws, there is no explicit ROLLBACK. While the calling code uses try/finally with client.release(), and pg.Pool does issue an implicit ROLLBACK when releasing a client with a pending transaction, relying on this implicit behavior is fragile and inconsistent with other transaction patterns in the codebase (e.g., migration files use explicit BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK in try/catch/finally).
